---
title: "Training and test data"
---

The [prediction-target page](prediction-targets.qmd) fixed three meanings of *new* for the corrected Natural Stories data. We now make one participant-held-out separation observable. The [**training set**](https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html) estimates every fitted quantity; the [**test set**](https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html) is used only to evaluate the resulting predictions.

The [residuals of a fitted regression](../regression-models/residuals.qmd) are observed-minus-fitted discrepancies on the observations used to estimate its coefficients. A flexible model can reduce those residuals by following features of the training responses that will not recur. Training fit thus cannot by itself estimate predictive loss for a reader absent during fitting.

We first state the separation rule, implement one participant-held-out Natural Stories target, and then inspect preprocessing leakage, split dependence, and reproducibility checks before treating the held-out score as evidence about new readers.

## The separation rule

Let $D_{\mathrm{train}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{test}}$ be disjoint collections of observations. A fitted predictor is

$$
\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}
=
\operatorname{Fit}(D_{\mathrm{train}}),
$$

and test loss is

$$
\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in D_{\mathrm{test}}}
L\left(y_i,\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}(x_i)\right).
$$

The subscript on $\widehat f$ is essential. Test responses must not influence the coefficients, predictor transformations, model choice, or any other fitted quantity used to produce their predictions.

## Participant-held-out validation target {#participant-held-out-validation-target}

The [Natural Stories dossier](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories-measurement-dossier)
defines one row as one retained button latency for a reader at a word position. The
[VTS](index.qmd#validation-target-specification) for this analysis is:

| VTS decision | present choice |
|:--|:--|
| split unit | participant; all of a reader's responses move together |
| score unit | response row on this page; participant weighting comes next |
| information set | word length, Google Books log unigram count, and GPT-3 word surprisal as defined in the [predictor provenance table](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories-measurement-dossier) | <!-- dqr-allow: reference-metadata -->
| quantities refit in each split | predictor means and [standard deviations](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd#definition), which measure predictor spread, then regression coefficients |
| transfer target | similarly sampled readers of these ten represented stories |

The following code loads the prepared Natural Stories table and keeps rows for which the response and all three predictors are finite. It then randomly shuffles the participant identifiers, assigns them in turn to five groups, uses the first group as the test set, and uses the other four groups for training. All responses from one participant receive the same group label. Predictor means, predictor standard deviations, and regression coefficients are estimated from the training rows before predictions are computed for the held-out rows.

We could use fewer groups, which would hold out more participants from each fit, or more groups, which would leave fewer participants in each test set. We choose five for the present analysis so that about four fifths of the participants estimate the fitted quantities and about one fifth evaluate them. The shuffled round-robin assignment balances participant counts to within one, but it does not balance response-row counts, reading speed, or any unobserved participant characteristic. The stated random seed makes this particular assignment reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: natural-train-test
#| message: false
#| warning: false

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
keep <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)
natural <- natural_all[keep, c(
  "participant_id", "story_id", "log_rt", "word_length",
  "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)]

participants <- sort(unique(as.character(natural$participant_id)))
set.seed(20261101)
participant_map <- data.frame(
  participant_id = sample(participants, length(participants)),
  fold = rep(seq_len(5), length.out = length(participants))
)
fold_lookup <- setNames(
  participant_map$fold, participant_map$participant_id
)
participant_fold <- unname(fold_lookup[natural$participant_id])
stopifnot(all(tapply(
  participant_fold, natural$participant_id,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
) == 1))

test <- participant_fold == 1
train <- !test
predictors <- c(
  "word_length", "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)

training_mean <- vapply(
  natural[train, predictors, drop = FALSE], mean, numeric(1)
)
training_sd <- vapply(
  natural[train, predictors, drop = FALSE], stats::sd, numeric(1)
)

training_matrix <- sweep(
  as.matrix(natural[train, predictors]), 2, training_mean, "-"
)
training_matrix <- sweep(training_matrix, 2, training_sd, "/")
test_matrix <- sweep(
  as.matrix(natural[test, predictors]), 2, training_mean, "-"
)
test_matrix <- sweep(test_matrix, 2, training_sd, "/")

fit <- stats::lm.fit(
  cbind("(Intercept)" = 1, training_matrix),
  natural$log_rt[train]
)
test_prediction <- drop(
  cbind("(Intercept)" = 1, test_matrix) %*% fit$coefficients
)

assignment <- data.frame(
  set = c("training", "test"),
  rows = c(sum(train), sum(test)),
  participants = c(
    length(unique(natural$participant_id[train])),
    length(unique(natural$participant_id[test]))
  ),
  stories = c(
    length(unique(natural$story_id[train])),
    length(unique(natural$story_id[test]))
  )
)
preprocessing <- data.frame(
  predictor = predictors,
  training_mean = unname(training_mean),
  training_sd = unname(training_sd)
)

prediction_decile <- cut(
  test_prediction,
  breaks = unique(quantile(
    test_prediction,
    probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11),
    names = FALSE
  )),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)
calibration <- data.frame(
  observed = natural$log_rt[test],
  predicted = test_prediction,
  decile = prediction_decile
)
calibration_bins <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(calibration, calibration$decile),
  function(rows) data.frame(
    mean_predicted = mean(rows$predicted),
    mean_observed = mean(rows$observed),
    se_observed = sd(rows$observed) / sqrt(nrow(rows))
  )
))

assignment
preprocessing

set.seed(20261102)
display_rows <- sample.int(
  nrow(calibration), min(12000, nrow(calibration))
)
ggplot2::ggplot(
  calibration[display_rows, ],
  ggplot2::aes(predicted, observed)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.45, alpha = 0.08, color = "grey30") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::geom_abline(
    slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    data = calibration_bins,
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = mean_predicted,
      y = mean_observed,
      ymin = mean_observed - 1.96 * se_observed,
      ymax = mean_observed + 1.96 * se_observed
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    width = 0,
    color = "#2B6CB0"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = calibration_bins,
    ggplot2::aes(mean_predicted, mean_observed),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 1.7,
    color = "#2B6CB0"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Held-out predicted log reading time",
    y = "Observed log reading time"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The training set contains `r format(assignment$rows[assignment$set == "training"], big.mark = ",")` responses from `r assignment$participants[assignment$set == "training"]` readers. The test set contains `r format(assignment$rows[assignment$set == "test"], big.mark = ",")` responses from `r assignment$participants[assignment$set == "test"]` readers. All `r unique(assignment$stories)` stories remain represented on both sides. Thus positions from every story, together with their lexical predictors, appear in training while different readers of those same stories appear in test. The target is a new reader of these ten stories rather than a new text.

The gray points show a reproducible display sample of raw held-out responses. The blue points and intervals summarize those responses within prediction deciles. This combines the raw test outcomes and the fitted model without using test responses to estimate the regression.

The deciles are defined by quantiles of the held-out predictions so each bin contains
roughly the same number of rows. Within a bin, the blue interval is the observed mean
plus or minus $1.96$ row-level standard errors. Recall that a [standard
error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd#deriving-the-standard-error-of-a-mean)
is the standard deviation of a specified estimator under a specified
repeated-sampling model. Here the estimator is the mean held-out log latency in
one prediction bin, and the working sampling units are response rows. Repeated
responses from the same participant and word position make that row-independence
calculation descriptive rather than a participant-level uncertainty analysis. It
is also not a predictive interval for a new response. Sampling at most 12,000 gray points changes only what is drawn;
the fit, bins, and printed summaries use every held-out row.

The mathematics-to-code correspondence is direct:

| mathematical object | code object |
|:--|:--|
| $D_{\mathrm{train}}$, $D_{\mathrm{test}}$ | logical vectors `train`, `test` |
| $\overline x_{\mathrm{train}}$, $s_{\mathrm{train}}$ | `training_mean`, `training_sd` |
| $\widehat f_{\mathrm{train}}$ | `fit` |
| $\widehat f_{\mathrm{train}}(x_i)$ | `test_prediction` |
| realized test responses $y_i$ | `natural$log_rt[test]` |

Thus the fitted function is estimated from random training data, while the displayed
`test_prediction` values are its estimates for this realized split.

## Leakage through preprocessing

[**Data leakage**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage) occurs when information from the test set influences a fitted decision that should have been made without it. Directly fitting on a test response is one case, but preprocessing can leak more quietly.

- Centering a predictor using the complete dataset lets held-out predictor values affect the training representation.
- Imputing a missing test response from a full-data mean uses held-out responses.
- Selecting predictors by their full-data response [correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd), the standardized covariance measuring linear association, consults the test set.
- Choosing a model because it has the best test score turns the test data into selection data.
- Averaging reading times over readers before holding readers out carries their responses into the target.

For a standardized predictor, the training mean $\overline{x}_{\mathrm{train}}$ and standard deviation $s_{\mathrm{train}}$ define

$$
z_i=\frac{x_i-\overline{x}_{\mathrm{train}}}{s_{\mathrm{train}}}
$$

for both training and test observations. The test data are not standardized separately, because that would change the coordinate system. The complete-data moments are also excluded, because they would make the training representation depend on held-out rows.

## One split and repeated decisions

A single split combines model performance with the composition of one test set. Increasing the test fraction provides more evaluation responses but fewer fitting responses; decreasing it has the opposite effect. Cross-validation rotates the test role so that every observation receives a held-out prediction.

The test set is also not a renewable source of decisions. If several specifications are compared on these responses and the best is selected, its reported score is optimistic. A three-way split or nested cross-validation keeps final test responses outside both coefficient fitting and model selection.

## Checking the separation

1. Which participants contribute responses to both sets in this split?
2. Which moments define the test-set predictor transformation?
3. Why does the calibration figure not estimate an omitted-story target?
4. What changes if the test responses guide model selection?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. None; the assertion after fold construction verifies that each participant has
   exactly one fold label.
2. The means and standard deviations estimated from training rows define both
   training and test coordinates.
3. Every story remains represented in training, so no story is absent.
4. The test set becomes selection data, and its score is optimistic as an estimate
   of the performance of the selected procedure.

</details>

## Recap and forward link

1. Participants, rather than rows, cross the training-test boundary.
2. Preprocessing and coefficients are learned from training data.
3. Display sampling and calibration summaries do not alter the fit.

The [previous page](prediction-targets.qmd#three-prediction-targets) fixed the
prediction unit; the [next page](predictive-loss.qmd#the-averaging-unit-is-part-of-the-target)
defines the numerical consequence assigned to these participant-held-out errors.
